ASRSN:1917846.n: The First Officer was flying and we had experienced a flap fail at 7,000 ft. about 12 miles out from the runway once the First Officer as called for flaps 30 degrees. We executed the go-around procedure and re-stabilized the aircraft. I had run the Flap Fail QRH procedure and returned to land with the flaps stuck at 20 degrees. As the Captain, I conducted the landing and performed a safe and uneventful landing with the assistance of my first officer. The CRJ-200 is known to have a flap fail issue and we were prepared in the event if anything was to go wrong. Aircraft require maintenance and to be looked at thoroughly to ensure that flap failure does not occur again.
ASRSN:1917846.s: The Captain and First Officer of a CRJ-200 experienced a flap failure at 7,000 feet while requesting 30 degrees, causing a go-around. After executing the QRH procedure, the Captain landed safely with flaps stuck at 20 degrees, noting the aircraft requires maintenance to prevent recurrence.

ASRSN:1917864.n: On final when selecting flaps 15, there was a flap drive caution. We executed a missed approach, ran the Emergency and Abnormal checklist and [advised ATC]. We made a call to the flight attendants, an announcement to the passengers, and consulted with Dispatch and Maintenance. We made a safe 10 degree flap landing. No limitations were exceeded. We landed close to our 45 minutes of reserve fuel. The tight fuel quantity added pressure to the situation. It has been my observation that there is often just enough fuel on many flights lately with not enough cushion to hold or go missed and troubleshoot issues. It would have been nice to have more fuel today to give us a bit more time to troubleshoot. On final to XXL in ZZZ we got a flap drive caution when selecting the flaps to 15. We flew the missed approach and ran the appropriate checklist. We [advised ATC], consulted with Dispatch and Maintenance and executed a flaps 10 landing on XXR.Dividing up tasks and coordinating with external sources allowed us to get on the ground in a timely fashion and reemphasized the importance of CRM. Despite that, we landed close to the 45 minutes reserve. It would have been nice to have more fuel available to us on departure.
ASRSN:1917864.s: The flight crew received a flap drive caution on final approach to XXL while selecting flaps 15, prompting a missed approach and checklist execution. They subsequently performed a safe flaps 10 landing on XXR with minimal reserve fuel, noting that tighter fuel margins increased pressure during the troubleshooting process.

ASRSN:1917894.n: While on a 1/2-1 NM final on the Visual Approach to Runway 07, the Pilot Flying in the right seat noted a flying drone above the aircraft at approximately 500 ft. I noticed a large black bird on the left side of the aircraft, just prior. I never saw the drone, and the Pilot Flying said he saw it briefly while focusing on the transition to land. We ensured our aircraft was clear of the drone, and landed uneventfully. Once on the ground, at a safe rollout, we quickly discussed what the Pilot Flying saw, and relayed it to the tower. Tower ensured the aircraft landing shortly behind us was aware. The Ground Controller collected our best description of the drone and its location. Nothing else significant to report.No suggestions. ORL tower and ground control coordinated very well.
ASRSN:1917894.s: The Pilot Flying in the right seat reported seeing a drone at 500 ft during a visual approach to Runway 07, while the narrator observed a bird. The crew landed uneventfully, notified the tower, and Ground Control coordinated with the following aircraft.

ASRSN:1917896.n: After takeoff and during gear retraction the Engine 2 Fire Level 3 Warning was triggered. I was the Pilot Monitoring (PM) at this time. The Pilot Flying (PF) continued climbing, I requested priority handling and reduced thrust on Engine 2 while the First Officer continued flying. After a slight reduction of thrust the Fire Warning ceased. After leveling the aircraft at 4,000 feet, I took control and became the Pilot Flying. We notified ATC of our situation and requested holding instructions. We assessed the situation and decided that the safest course of action would be to return to ZZZ.In the hold, we dumped fuel (which required constant recalculations since the fuel system was in Manual resulting in the fuel dump not stopping at the FMS Dump To Gross Weight), sent an ACARS to company regarding our situation, and returned to land via ILS7R. The Tower had the emergency vehicles on standby, though we didn't make this request. After making an uneventful landing we proceeded to taxi to our parking gate under normal power. We were alerted by the Engine 2 Fire Warning at approximately 200-300 feet. Possible bleed air leak or fault in the Engine 2 Fire Loop. Reduced thrust on Engine 2, took over as Pilot Flying, requested priority handling, dumped fuel, returned to land. Diligent maintenance corrections. I was told by a Maintenance rep that the Engine Fire warning went off '54' times on a previous leg. Immediately after rotation on takeoff at approximately 200 feet, a Level 3 Engine 2 fire presented itself for approximately 1 minute. ZZZ Tower was then notified of the situation. As we climbed up to the acceleration altitude and by this time the L3 message had cleared itself after slightly reducing power on the #2 engine. We ran the appropriate QRH checklist , requested a hold @ ZZZ Vor and finalized our decision to return to ZZZ. We then confirmed permission to dump fuel with the Tower for approximately 15 mins. After dumping was accomplished we returned to ZZZ via the ILS XR approach. A normal landing was accomplished and since there was no more fire indication present. A normal taxi to the gate was conducted. In conclusion, maintenance had detected a hole in the #2 bleed blowing hot air on the A loop fire detector.
ASRSN:1917896.s: The crew experienced a Level 3 Engine 2 fire warning at 200 feet after takeoff, which cleared after reducing thrust. They returned to ZZZ, dumped fuel, and landed safely; maintenance later found a bleed air leak blowing hot air on the fire detector.

ASRSN:1917899.n: Aircraft received landing gear airground fail message on short final. Performed go around, ran QRH, came back to ZZZMaintain vigilance for changing conditions. Aircraft received landing air ground fail on short final. Performed go around and QRH and went back to ZZZ to land.Maintain vigilance for changing conditions.
ASRSN:1917899.s: The aircraft received a landing gear air/ground fail message on short final, prompting a go-around and QRH execution. The crew subsequently returned to ZZZ to land safely.

ASRSN:1917956.n: Captain reported aircraft was too hot to board passengers, conditioned air was INOP, and APU was on MEL, so he would refuse the aircraft unless he could reactivate the MELed APU briefly to cool down aircraft. I went out to talk to the Captain to get a clearer direction on what he wanted and he said he was going to turn the APU on to cool down the aircraft. We informed the Captain that the APU was on MEL for fire loop not testing and exhaust cone issues, and that would reactivate the APU from MEL. Maintenance Control was also trying to clarify whether this would even be possible without a fire watch. Went outside to APU to inspect and me being in Management, to call maintenance personnel for support, and control to figure out a course of action when I heard the APU fire up. No maintenance personnel was present in Flight Deck or Outside aircraft, no fire watch personnel was present, APU was placarded INOP, and MEL was complied with previously. I called my OM on duty to report this and see what steps I needed to take, or if he thought this was a compliance issue, and he told me it was out of our hands at that point as it had already been reactivated by the pilot. I then witnessed boarding of the aircraft with passengers (with a fire loop issue on APU) after the Controller told pilot he should not board passengers with the APU running that was deferred for that. Later the door was shut with APU still running, then APU was shut off and aircraft departed gate for flight. I feel the Pilot (whether it be the Captain or First Officer (FO) I cannot be certain) performed maintenance by reactivating a deferred item on MEL that could have caused a safety issue without maintenance or fire watch present. Maintenance was not asked to put APU back into placarded INOP status to continue to comply with MEL before aircraft departed. I felt I needed to report this, as I felt this was off compliance wise, and a grey area that I have not dealt with before. The Controller I was communicating with, including Operations felt the same way in communication with what was going on and with the Pilots.
ASRSN:1917956.s: A Captain reactivated a deferred APU with fire loop and exhaust cone issues to cool the aircraft without maintenance or a fire watch present. Passengers boarded while the APU ran, and the aircraft departed after the APU was shut off, raising concerns that the pilot performed unauthorized maintenance.

ASRSN:1917957.n: Aircraft experienced an smoke, odor, or fume event on Day 0. On Day 1 Troubleshooting performed on [Job Card 1] determined APU was possible cause resulting in APU and APU bleed valve both being placed on MEL. On logbook sheet #XXXXXXX Day 2, [Maintenance Control] updates with request to accomplish APU SOF TS (Troubleshooting) card, APU inlet Wash, APU Load comp wash and [Job Card 4] to burn out ECS (Environmental Control System) before releasing APU back into service. On Day 3 under same logbook sheet XXXXXXX, [APU SOF] troubleshooting performed and APU found to be leaking at Scroll and FCU (Fuel Control Unit), but unable to repair so deferral continues with logbook sheet XXXXXXX1 created for reinspect. Logbook sheet XXXXXXX2 created Day 3 to leave APU on MEL until repair can be made and ECS decontamination and load comp wash can be C/W (Complied With). Day 3 logbook sheet XXXXXXX3 created to accomplish APU SOF TS card again after APU found leaking. (On Day 4, after discovery of leaking APU scroll housing and FCU (on Day 3) APU bleed valve was reactivated and APU was placed back in service by Employee with no repair performed.) [Job Card 2] APU SOF TS, Cleaning of APU intake, Wash APU Load Compressor, and ECS decontamination have not been accomplished. No repair to the APU was made to return it to serviceable condition after findings on Day 3. APU was used in service from Day until [overnight maintenance] was completed on Day 5 and the APU was repaired and [inspection] was accomplished. To be clear, the APU MEL was cleared and an unserviceable APU was placed back in service and used [for a period of 7 days].
ASRSN:1917957.s: Maintenance personnel returned an unserviceable APU with known leaks to service without repair or required cleaning for seven days. The APU was eventually repaired and inspected on Day 5 after being used while deferred on the MEL.

ASRSN:1917965.n: We were on a test flight after maintenance, Captain and First Officer altimeters variate by 900 ft., airspeed different by 60 kts. We returned to airport, switched from Tower to Departure then back to Tower for uneventful landing. Called Maintenance and they blew out blocked static/pitot system blockage. The aircraft was parked outside with the pitot and static port covers NOT installed for a week. Also aircraft was washed and waxed. l believe that a bug or wax entered the system. In the future I will insist on a hangar or covers on pitot/static ports.
ASRSN:1917965.s: During a post-maintenance test flight, the Captain and First Officer experienced significant altimeter and airspeed discrepancies caused by a blocked static/pitot system. The crew returned for an uneventful landing after maintenance cleared the blockage, which the pilot attributed to bugs or wax entering the exposed ports while the aircraft was parked outside.

ASRSN:1917983.n: On Date I was conducting my AMEL Commercial Check ride out of ZZZ. During our time in the practice area conducting our maneuvers per the Airman Certification Standards (ACS). All mechanical functions of the aircraft had been functioning at a normal capacity and I had to demonstrate my engine shutdown and air restart under Task A of the Multiengine operations of the ACS. During this procedure all memory items and checklist were used to secure the failed engine. During the restart procedure we were unable to successfully restart the inoperative engine and [advised ATC]. It was decided that the check ride was now over and I made a positive transfer of controls over the other Pilot while I ran the checklist in our QRH for or gear extension. We proceeded direct to ZZZ1 as our intended place for an emergency landing. We were able to successfully land without any injuries or damage to the aircraft or any property. After proper shut down procedures we exited the aircraft and performed a visual inspection of the failed engine. Upon the inspection it was noticed the prop did not come out of feather. I believe the problem was due to that prop not being exercised in and out of feather paired with a weak starter. During our time in the air I believe both pilots followed appropriate actions and proper procedures to ensure the safety of flight and a well executed landing.
ASRSN:1917983.s: During a commercial check ride, the pilot could not restart an inoperative engine due to a propeller failing to unfeather, likely caused by lack of exercise and a weak starter. The crew executed an emergency landing at ZZZ1 with no injuries or damage.

ASRSN:1918012.n: After passing the ZZZZZ intersection on the approach the autopilot and navigation system failed. I reset the navigation system and returned to course and altitude and hand flew the approach to the airport.
ASRSN:1918012.s: The pilot experienced autopilot and navigation system failures after passing the ZZZZZ intersection on approach. The pilot reset the navigation system, returned to course and altitude, and hand-flew the approach to the airport.

ASRSN:1918015.n: Cruising at FL320 there was a sudden loss of the following:Pressurization IntercomLeft PFDFlap failSpeed brake failElevator trim failLeft PTT failRoll failAn immediate descent was initiated, entering thicker air the plane was becoming uncontrollable until standby pitch trim was selected, then a fast clean long landing with only brakes to stop causing excessive heat and landing gear damage. Unfortunately the emergency checklist only covers one failure at a time and each adds a percentage to the landing distance. Unable to calculate landing performance due to multiple system failures.
ASRSN:1918015.s: During cruise at FL320, the crew experienced simultaneous failures of pressurization, flight controls, and displays, rendering the aircraft uncontrollable until standby pitch trim was selected. The resulting emergency landing caused excessive heat and landing gear damage, as the checklist could not address multiple simultaneous failures to calculate performance.

ASRSN:1918025.n: I was spraying a field in the afternoon around XA:40pm. The field was almost complete and I was just finishing the final passes when I hit the powerline.
ASRSN:1918025.s: A pilot spraying a field in the afternoon struck a powerline while completing final passes. The incident occurred around 14:40 as the operation was nearly finished.

ASRSN:1918035.n: I issued Aircraft X the RNAV XX approach at ZZZ. After the pilot was established on the approach, I issued a communications change to contact ZZZ FSS. After scanning the ZZZ area again, I realized the aircraft was in a turn NE bound, no longer established on the approach, heading into a 7000 ft. MIA. The aircraft made a series of maneuvering turns in the 7000 ft. MIA and climbed and then descended between roughly 6000 ft. and 4200 ft. I issued a low altitude alert and a climb to 7000 ft. and my D-side instructed ZZZ FSS to issue a low altitude alert as well. Neither ZZZ FSS or I was able to reach the pilot, and attempted to have an overflying aircraft broadcast on XXX.X, as well as guard frequency to issue the climb to the pilot.No one was able to get a hold of the pilot and the aircraft didn't climb, but eventually the pilot re-established themselves on the approach and made a safe landing. The pilot never contacted ZZZ FSS, but instead finally transmitted on our freq XXX.X to close out their flight plan on the ground at ZZZ. No recommendations. This appeared to be caused by a mixture of pilot navigational error, possible equipment issues, and a lack of familiarization with the area/approach.
ASRSN:1918035.s: An air traffic controller issued an RNAV XX approach to Aircraft X at ZZZ, but the pilot deviated into a 7000 ft MIA and could not be reached on multiple frequencies. The aircraft eventually re-established the approach and landed safely, attributed to pilot navigational error, possible equipment issues, and lack of area familiarization.

ASRSN:1918065.n: Upon taxi out to Runway XXR at intersection XX for takeoff, the Captain and I accomplished the before takeoff checklist in its entirety. Within this, the takeoff reference speeds, as well as stabilizer trim and reduced thrust setting were all confirmed per the FOM. (Note, they had dropped out once before). We were then given an ATC reroute while taxiing, for a different fix beginning after the SID, which was sent by CPDLC. The change was loaded into the FMC via CPDLC upload. We even noted, that there was no checklist for such change, since this was no change to any ORCA segment nor a runway change. On takeoff roll, after the 100 kt. callout, I first noticed that there were no reference speeds on the speed tape, only the MCP bugged V2 value and the L/D speed for both current flap and next flap setting. I quickly grabbed the take off data sheet next to me, and called out, 'V1;' and 'ROTATE;' on time. During takeoff roll, after 100 kt. call, realized no Vr V1 reference speeds on PFDs. FO (First Officer) (PM (Pilot Monitoring)) referenced takeoff data and called out V1, VR and takeoff completed normally.
ASRSN:1918065.s: During takeoff roll, the First Officer noticed missing V1 and Vr reference speeds on the PFDs after a CPDLC route upload. The crew used the takeoff data sheet to call speeds manually, resulting in a normal takeoff despite the display anomaly.

ASRSN:1918067.n: On takeoff in ZZZ we received an IRS Master Caution light at approximately 110 kts. The takeoff was continued. The First Officer lost his attitude and heading information on his PFD. The SID and departure clearance were complied with. Upon reaching a safe altitude we ran the IRS Fault QRH 2.110.9 FM. Dispatch and Maintenance Control were consulted on the ramifications of the fault and the loss of associated systems. Because of the IRS fault we were not able to re-establish function of the Autopilot. Without the Autopilot, RVSM airspace operations were not available, nor could they be accommodated by relevant ARTCC sectors. Our flight could not be completed to ZZZ1 in non-RVSM airspace with the fuel onboard, in consideration of the weather and airspace congestion to be anticipated in ZZZ1. A diversion to ZZZ2 was completed in consideration of the maintenance facilities, aircraft availability, and passenger services available. A plan of action on arrival was made, two hours prior to landing with Dispatch and Maintenance Control for the completion of the flight to ZZZ1. Thereafter the lead Flight Attendant and I made relevant announcements and query requests from passengers. Maintenance was able to swap out the faulty IRS, but not in time before impacting weather began to severely impact the ZZZ1 operation so a decision to swap aircraft was initiated. The original plan of action to complete the flight to ZZZ1 was not completed due to misinformed Customer Service Agents. On takeoff roll in ZZZ we received an IRS Master Caution light at approximately 110 kts. The takeoff was continued. The First Officer lost his attitude and heading information on his PFD. The SID and departure clearance were complied with by the Pilot Flying who had all normal indications. Upon reaching a safe altitude we ran the IRS Fault QRH 2.110.9 FM. Dispatch and Maintenance Control were consulted on the ramifications of the fault and the loss of associated systems. Because of the IRS fault we were not able to re-establish function of the Autopilot. Without the Autopilot, RVSM airspace operations were not available, nor could they be accommodated by needed ARTCC sectors. Our flight could not be completed in non-RVSM airspace with the fuel onboard, in consideration of the weather and airspace congestion to be anticipated in ZZZ1. A diversion to ZZZ2 was completed in consideration of the maintenance facilities, aircraft availability, and passenger services available. A plan of action was made two hours prior to landing with Dispatch and Maintenance Controll for the completion of the flight to ZZZ1. Thereafter the lead flight attendant and Captain made relevant announcements and answered requests from passengers. Maintenance was able to swap out the faulty IRS, but not in time before bad weather began to severely impact the ZZZ1 operation so a decision to swap aircraft was initiated.
ASRSN:1918067.s: During takeoff from ZZZ, an IRS fault caused the First Officer to lose attitude and heading information, disabling the Autopilot and RVSM capability. The crew diverted to ZZZ2 due to fuel and airspace constraints, but ultimately swapped aircraft because maintenance could not repair the IRS before severe weather impacted ZZZ1.

ASRSN:1918081.n: On final approach to XXL in ZZZZ, out of 5,000 ft. and cleared for the approach, the first officer armed the approach mode. Once armed, we received multiple EICAS messages (3 pages) of system failures. I lost background lighting and multiple instruments. I looked up at the electrical panel and noted the STBY PWR OFF Light illuminated. After requesting priority handling, I handed the Paper QRH to the International Relief Officer and instructed her to read the Standby Power Off checklist. We complied with the checklist and continued the approach to an uneventful landing.On rollout, I took control of the aircraft, and through 100 kts., felt the airplane being sluggish. I stated I thought we had blown tires, as our inboard tires had no anti-skid protection. We cleared the runway, and noted the break temp monitors were at 9 on my outboard brakes. I called Tower to ensure services were enroute, and wanted them to focus on our main landing gear in case of fire. Once ensured there was no fire, I contacted Ops, Dispatch, Maintenance Control to make everyone aware of our situation. After approximately 30 minutes I was informed that all 8 main tires were flat. Air stairs were brought to the aircraft, and all passengers and crew egressed with no injuries. We were taken by bus to the main terminal.Before leaving the aircraft, an ELB write up was accomplished. Upon further investigation of the logbook's history, I see there was a similar write up of a 'hard power transfer' when the approach mode was selected with multiple EICAS messages. In their case, they never lost STBY PWR, as in mine. Seems there was an electric anomaly with this jet that was never found by Maintenance. In my opinion, the paper QRH should not be removed from our aircraft, as it was the fastest means for us to accomplish a lengthy checklist before landing, as this problem presented itself at a very inopportune moment on approach.This is an addendum to a previous report. It was brought to my attention after landing that the speed brakes failed to deploy, and the crew missed that fact with all our attention focused on failed systems, checklists, and flying the airplane. Upon landing my focus was squarely on keeping the airplane tracking the runway center line. In the end, with the length of runway, I do not believe the speed brakes were a factor in the final outcome of the flight.
ASRSN:1918081.s: The flight crew experienced multiple system failures and standby power loss on final approach to XXL, leading to an uneventful landing with eight flat tires and failed speed brakes. The pilot attributed the electrical anomaly to a known maintenance issue and credited the paper QRH for enabling safe checklist completion.

ASRSN:1918086.n: Experienced moderate turbulence caused by convective activity. Convective activity painted below was 1 mile or less in circumference. Aircraft climbed approximately 400 ft. Stick shaker momentarily activated. Deselected autopilot and autothrottles, hand flew aircraft back down to 36000 ft., reengaged automation. Duration of event estimated between 30 seconds and 1 minute. Flight attendants were seated not injured. Informed us of 3 passengers injured with bumps and bruises. Continued to destination ZZZZ. 6 more passengers reported similar injuries before uneventful landing. Maintenance write-up for moderate turbulence cleared by Maintenance in ZZZZ. This was a morning flight to ZZZZ. On climb out there were some cumulus clouds low, but we were above that very quickly and at that hour (XA-XBAM), nothing had developed into storms. We had the seatbelt sign off, but upon entering a cirrus layer, had turned it back on. We were just past waypoint ZZZZZ at 36000 ft. in IMC when the Captain alerted me to a very small cell close ahead that neither of us had detected thus far. I had my radar tilted -2 but did not see anything displayed. I know Name had his radar displayed and tilted down as well. He also had WSI displayed on his side and nothing was depicted. It had been mostly smooth with nothing painting on the radar. Name immediately had the flight attendants seated and thankfully they all were seated during the event and no one was injured. We tried to turn away from it (left turn) but still ended up penetrating it for about 30 seconds to 1 minute. The depiction of it on radar at this point was small and round. We experienced moderate turbulence with one strong upgust. Our speed staying at bugged speed, but the stall tape came up to our current speed causing the stick shaker to go off for about 5-10 seconds. Name turned off the AP and kept the aircraft level and with forward pressure. His hand was on the thrust levers and we ended up at 36,400 ft. I had turned the engine start selectors both to flight. Once we were out of it, Name verbalized he was getting back to 36000 ft. and we re-engaged the autopilot. We made contact with the flight attendants and were advised the cabin was a mess because this happened during the service. There was food, drinks, trays and broken glass throughout the galley and cabin. We asked about injuries, but nothing was reported until about 20 minutes later. We were told that 3 passengers had some bumps and bruises, but were otherwise fine. Over the next hour, 6 other passengers were identified to have bruises and scrapes, but nothing significant from what we were told. Two flights attendants in the rear told us two female passengers who came forward with injuries were not wearing their seat belts. They indicated the passengers had told them they had not been wearing their seat belts. Next we had a conference call with Maintenance and Dispatch over Satcom to advise them of the incident and request paramedics to meet us in ZZZZ. Through our discussion with Maintenance and referencing the FOM it was determined that we encountered moderate turbulence. We made a maintenance entry and an inspection was done by Maintenance in ZZZZ. There was no other weather after this one isolated storm. The rest of the way was smooth. I don't know for sure, but suspect it was an isolated column that built below us very rapidly and we met it at just the right time. Upon arrival in ZZZZ, we were met with EMT. Five passengers elected to be seen by the EMT professionals and we found out afterward that one passenger went to the hospital for back pain. The flight attendants told us this particular passenger was one of the ones not wearing a seatbelt. We flew the ZZZZ-ZZZ flight back and there was no convective activity and no storms. It was mostly clear and smooth. There were a couple low convective clouds around ZZZZZ1, but that was it. It was very odd, because normally there would be more areas of convection/storms and they would build into the afternoon.
ASRSN:1918086.s: During climb past waypoint ZZZZZ at 36,000 ft, the crew encountered an undetected convective cell causing moderate turbulence and a momentary stick shaker activation. The event resulted in nine passenger injuries, primarily to those not wearing seatbelts, and required a maintenance inspection upon arrival at ZZZZ.

ASRSN:1918095.n: While conducting an LCA candidate assessment observation. I was not the Captain of record. I was in the jump-seat, the Captain was informed that a Flight Attendant had placed a computer in a Thermal Containment Bag. This was due to a passenger informing Flight Attendant of computer that was warm. The Captain then informed Flight Operations and Maintenance of issue. My understanding is the Thermal Containment Bag was removed from aircraft with the computer inside. The Thermal Containment Bag was replaced before departure. Our Purser informed us that a passenger had mentioned to one of the Flight Attendants that their computer had gotten warm on their previous flight. The Flight Attendant might have misunderstood and she put it in the Thermal Containment Bag. Regardless, we had to write up the used Thermal Containment Bag and have Maintenance/Operations remove the computer and figure out what to do with the computer.
ASRSN:1918095.s: A Flight Attendant placed a passenger's warm computer in a Thermal Containment Bag during pre-flight, likely misunderstanding a report about a previous flight. The Captain notified Operations and Maintenance, resulting in the removal of the bag and computer before departure.

ASRSN:1918108.n: Operation of flight XXX from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1 B763. On final approach in ZZZ1 about 18 miles from the runway at 5000 ft., we were cleared for the ILS XXL. Upon pushing the APP button to arm the approach mode, a complete loss of standby power on both AC and DC busses commenced. 3 pages of Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System (EICAS) messages appeared and various aircraft systems failed. The Captain called for standby power off checklist to the RP. The checklist called for various flap settings and what worked vs what was lost as a result. Flaps were commanded to 20 and a REF speed of 170 was needed for the approach. Upon touchdown the inboard tires blew and the outboard tires deflated due to temperatures exceeding limits. This was due to the lack of auto brakes and anti-skid systems. Crash Fire Rescue was called to the aircraft, water was sprayed to cool down the brakes and a bus with air stairs was used to egress passengers. No fire or injuries to report.
ASRSN:1918108.s: During the ILS approach of a B763 to ZZZ1, a total standby power loss caused multiple system failures and disabled auto-brakes and anti-skid. Consequently, tire blowouts occurred on touchdown due to excessive heat, requiring fire rescue cooling and bus egress, though no injuries or fires resulted.

ASRSN:1918144.n: ZZZ Tower Controller cleared us to cross Runway XXL on [Taxiway] X. As we crossed Runway XXL the same controller cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff on Runway XXL. The controller then proceeded to give departure sequence updates over the frequency (XXX.X). We transmitted we were on the runway. Aircraft Y was finally able to tell the controller he saw us and was holding position. The controller then stated to Aircraft Y that he had indeed cleared us to cross [Runway] XXL and that he had made a mistake. The flight was scheduled as an afternoon turn to ZZZ1-ZZZ-ZZZ1. I was the First Officer and was the pilot flying to ZZZ--this event occurred on the ground during the taxi to the ZZZ ramp. After landing on [Runway] XXR (approx XA10), ZZZ Tower instructed to roll to the end, taxi left on Taxiway Z, Y, X--hold short of [Runway] XXL at [Taxiway] X, and to monitor Tower XXX.X. After several departures, we were cleared to taxi to the ramp via [Taxiway] X, cleared to cross [Runway] XXL at [Taxiway] X, and notified traffic will be holding in position. At approximately the time our nose gear crossed the centerline of the runway, ZZZ Tower cleared Aircraft Y to takeoff and was immediately acknowledged by the Aircraft Y crew. Recognizing we were not going to be clear, I tried to notify Tower that we were still on the runway--I don't think he heard my call, he was giving a takeoff sequence to several aircraft awaiting takeoff. After ZZZ Tower finished reading the sequence, Aircraft Y told the controller that he cleared them for takeoff while 'Aircraft X was still on the runway'. The Tower controller acknowledged the mistake and re-cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff.
ASRSN:1918144.s: The First Officer reported that while crossing Runway XXL at Taxiway X, ZZZ Tower cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff, creating a runway incursion. The controller admitted the error after Aircraft Y held position, and the flight continued to the ramp without incident.

ASRSN:1918156.n: Possible fuel leak, followed QRH procedure to an inflight shut down. [Requested priority handling] and diverted to ZZZ1.[Cause:] None as far as crew is aware. Procedure followed.
ASRSN:1918156.s: The crew suspected a fuel leak, followed the QRH for an inflight shutdown, and diverted to ZZZ1 with priority handling. The reporter stated no cause was known and procedures were followed.

ASRSN:1918166.n: Upon receiving aircraft with the APU left running at gate for flight in ZZZ Flight Attendant NAME immediately noticed a pungent musty/wet sock odor around row 11. As we discussed the smell it continued to get stronger. I called maintenance and made a notation in the aircraft maintenance log. Gate agent noticed the smell when he came down to the aircraft as well as the maintenance personnel. The odor continued to get stronger as time passed. We were not on the aircraft for more than 10-15 minutes. Passengers never boarded the aircraft. Approximately 20-30 minutes after deplaning, all crew members had brief symptoms. Three of us had very mild headache, one had a mild sore throat, one had slight dizziness. All symptoms lasted about 10 minutes. I queried all crew member if medical attention was required, all confirmed they were OK to continue to ZZZ1. No medical attention was required for flight crew. The prompt identification and action of Flight Attendant [name] played a significant role in identifying a health problem for anybody boarding the aircraft.
ASRSN:1918166.s: Flight attendants and maintenance personnel detected a strong musty odor on an aircraft with the APU running at the gate before passengers boarded. The smell caused brief mild symptoms in the crew, but no medical attention was required, and the flight proceeded after the issue was identified.

ASRSN:1918170.n: Taking off on Runway XXR. Low speed reject for PSEU (Proximity Electronics Unit) caution light. Taxied off of runway. Captain called maintenance and we were advised to return to gate. Maintenance took the aircraft out of service.
ASRSN:1918170.s: The crew rejected takeoff on Runway XXR due to a PSEU caution light. Maintenance was called, advised the aircraft to return to the gate, and subsequently took it out of service.

ASRSN:1918183.n: We brought this airplane from ZZZ1 with the original Bleed Valve 2 MEL that occurred during preflight in ZZZ1. During departure from ZZZ XXR, passing 4,000 feet MSL (estimated), amber Bleed Valve #1 Fault occurred. Completed Normal checklist items, then complied with ECAM. ECAM tried resetting Bleed Valve 1, did not reset. Complied with ECAM, then QRH. Leveled off at 10,000 feet MSL due to no pressurization. Slowed to 250 KIAS, tried resetting Bleed Valve 1, reset worked. Tried to accelerate to 320 KIAS and Bleed Valve 1 faulted again. Requested priority handling with plan to return to ZZZ. Complied with ECAM, QRH, then slowed back to 250 KIAS. Reset Bleed Valve 1, to have pressurization, maintained that configuration until landing with no Bleed Valve 1 fault. After landing complied with ECAM, QRH. Initially was pilot monitoring, transferred duties and flew an ILS XYL approach at ZZZ. Climbing through approximately 4,000 feet we experienced a Bleed Valve 1 Fault amber ECAM message. Bleed Valve 2 was inop due to an MEL. We were cleared to 14,000 feet and were climbing. With no pressurization capabilities we decided to level at 10,000 feet. We finished all normal checklist items and slowed to 250 kts. When we pulled the power back and ran the ECAM items it initially reset. We then sped up to 320 kts. with the high power setting we again got the Bleed Valve 1 fault ECAM message again. We followed all ECAM instructions and QRH procedures. Unable to fly the plane without pressurization we [requested priority handling] and returned to ZZZ. We swapped duties as Pilot Monitoring and Pilot Flying the Captain made the landing.
ASRSN:1918183.s: The crew departed ZZZ XXR with Bleed Valve 2 inoperative and experienced a Bleed Valve 1 fault at 4,000 feet, causing loss of pressurization. They leveled at 10,000 feet, returned to ZZZ, and landed after maintaining the valve reset at 250 KIAS.

ASRSN:1918187.n: Due to a fuel system indication malfunction we needed to land at a field other than our primary or alternate in accordance with company checklists and operating procedures. MD-11 Fuel system indications became unreliable. [No suggestions.] Applied checklists and executed as discussed with Crew, Flight Operations and Maintenance. MD-11 tank 2 fuel indicators became unrealizable and precluded a safe oceanic transit so we diverted to ZZZZ1 in accordance with MD-11 checklists and Company recommendations. As a crew we needed to dump 36,000 pounds of fuel at FL 320, 218 NM's east of ZZZZZ. This fuel dump was required to get below max landing weight for the airframe. Cause - Material or system degradation
ASRSN:1918187.s: The MD-11 crew diverted to ZZZZ1 due to unreliable fuel system indications in tank 2, which precluded safe oceanic transit. They dumped 36,000 pounds of fuel at FL 320 to meet maximum landing weight limits, attributing the issue to material or system degradation.

ASRSN:1918188.n: Lost RT Hydraulic system on approach, complied with QRH (Quick Reference Handbook), requested priority handling and landed on Runway XXR at ZZZ. On approach at 5,000 feet ILS XXR, we lost the Right Hydraulic System. First Officer was Flying Pilot. Captain ran the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) while we received radar vectors back around for the approach. Checklist complete, came back around for an uneventful landing, except for the fact that Captain requested priority handling as a precaution. He took the controls and landed the airplane
ASRSN:1918188.s: The Captain and First Officer lost the Right Hydraulic System at 5,000 feet during an ILS approach to Runway XXR at ZZZ. After completing the QRH and receiving radar vectors, the Captain took control and executed an uneventful landing with priority handling.

ASRSN:1918196.n: Enroute flight crew conferenced called with fuel quantity issues / approximately 8k light / Maintenance Control, Tech, Duty Officer all on call. Unable to clear issue with reset of system. [Flight] diverted to ZZZZ1 dumped 36k fuel.
ASRSN:1918196.s: The enroute flight crew contacted Maintenance Control regarding an 8,000 lb fuel quantity discrepancy that could not be resolved by resetting the system. The aircraft was diverted to ZZZZ1 and dumped 36,000 lb of fuel.

ASRSN:1918218.n: When in our initial descent with Atlanta Center, we were given the clearance to maintain 290 knots and we were cleared to offset if needed to avoid wake turbulence for what they called a B767. In actuality, it was a larger B747 inbound into GSP. At approximately 12,500 feet MSL, we began to encounter wake turbulence. We began asking for an offset to the left knowing that the departure corridor was just off of our left wing by a few miles. With the wake turbulence becoming worse and the possibility of an upset, we turned approximately 15 degrees left off course and I used a radio transmission to get the attention of the CLT Approach Controller. She had another aircraft 'turn left immediately' to increase separation. We were then told to report level at 10,000 feet MSL, which we complied with. We were about 1.5 to 2 NM offset to the left for quite a few miles till told to proceed direct to RAYCE (the IAF) for the visual to Runway 22 by Greer Approach. Once headed for the approach fix, the rest of the flight continued normally.
ASRSN:1918218.s: During initial descent to GSP, the crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a B747 at 12,500 feet while cleared to maintain 290 knots. The pilot executed a 15-degree left offset to avoid an upset, prompting ATC to issue separation instructions and a level-off at 10,000 feet before resuming the approach.

ASRSN:1918233.n: At approximately XA00L, the First Officer and I boarded Aircraft X in ZZZZ. The First Officer immediately commented on the very-heavy dirty-sock odor in the cockpit, I agreed, and confirmed that the cabin was significantly affected as well. I asked the inflight crew to give their assessment, and they all agreed that we should not board under these conditions. I advised local maintenance about the issue. Maintenance confirmed the presence of the odor, and was able to clear the odor without an engine run and by deferring the APU Bleed. I made the appropriate logbook entry and completed the Odor Event form in the logbook.After starting both engines, the odor was not present. We departed Gate X in ZZZZ and were climbing through approximately 2,000 ft. MSL when the odor returned, though not to the same degree as at the gate in ZZZZ. We had climbed through an extremely thin layer of haze with extremely light precipitation. The First Officer commented that the odor was affecting him considerably, so as PM (Pilot Monitoring) I advised ATC of the odor event and requested a PPOS hold to assess the situation. Instead, ATC gave us a heading and advised that we would be vectored.The First Officer stated that he was not able to continue with the odor, as it was affecting him physically. Because we were overweight, I decided on a diversion to ZZZZ1, and contacted Dispatch via SATCOM to confirm my intention. After Dispatch concurred, I advised inflight about the diversion with a Code Yellow, and made an announcement to the customers. ATC cleared us to ZZZZ1 and asked if we were [requesting priority]. I replied that we were not, but ATC said they were [giving us priority handling] on our behalf, if I remember correctly, to 'get us into ZZZZ1.'We referenced the FOM and QRH procedures for an Odor Event and Overweight Landing, respectively. We set up for the longer [Runway] XX at ZZZZ1. I assigned myself as PF (Pilot Flying) to continue the flight. I landed at ZZZZ1 with a V/S of less than 100FPM. We were met at the gate by CFR (Crash Fire Rescue), and confirmed that there was no smoke present per CFR inquiry. I did not understand why CFR was asking me this question, but then realized that I may have stated an odor or fumes event to ATC, which would explain the [priority handling] on our behalf.We were also met by local maintenance, to whom I provided a detailed account of the Odor Event beginning in ZZZZ and the Overweight Landing in ZZZZ1. I made the appropriate logbook entries for the Odor Event and Overweight Landing, and completed another Odor Event form in the logbook.The First Officer contacted [Medical Services]. Paramedics arrived at the aircraft to evaluate the First Officer, who was removed from the pairing.I had several conversations with the Duty Chief Pilot about the event, and was initially told we would be overnighting in ZZZZ1. However, the entire crew, except the First Officer, was reassigned to operate from ZZZZ1 to ZZZ. I confirmed that all crewmembers were fit to fly, and we operated Aircraft Y on a different aircraft to ZZZ.
ASRSN:1918233.s: The flight crew diverted Aircraft X from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 due to a recurring odor event that physically affected the First Officer, requiring an overweight landing. The First Officer was medically removed from duty, while the remaining crew reassigned to operate a different aircraft to ZZZ.

ASRSN:1918237.n: The aircraft we were flying had experienced an odor event on the previous flight. The Auxiliary Power Unit was deferred and the aircraft went back into service for our flight. The flight was uneventful however on the descent. I'm unsure of what altitude it started. We smelled the 'Dirty Sock Smell'. The cockpit jump seat was occupied and all of us in the cockpit smelled it. We shut pack one off and shut the cross bleed and the smell dissipated. We landed without any further incident. The inflight crew did not smell anything.
ASRSN:1918237.s: The flight crew experienced a "Dirty Sock Smell" during descent on an aircraft with a deferred APU from a previous odor event. They shut off pack one and cross bleed, which dissipated the smell, allowing for a safe landing while the inflight crew reported no odor.

ASRSN:1918245.n: Upon entering the [aircraft] from the jetbridge, I noticed a foul odor in the forward galley and cockpit. APU Bleed Air and Pack 1 were turned off. The smell dissipated. There were no previous logbook write-ups for similar issues. While performing the walkaround I noticed the PC Air was hooked up, and we continued to use that for cabin climate control. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the odor issue and company protocol. We elected to minimize use of the APU and continued our [preparation].We experienced a strong foul odor during takeoff and climb. We referenced the FOM and FCOM (Flight Crew Operations Manual) 2 odor isolation guidance. I selected PACK 1 off and closed the crossbleed valve as per the procedure.As time went on, I continued to smell the odor, though not as strong as the takeoff and initial climb. Following a restroom break, I returned to the flight deck and the smell was very apparent. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed our condition, options and symptoms, and [queried] the cabin crew. We decided it was safe to continue to our destination. The aircraft was written up for cabin odors and ZZZ Tech Ops met the aircraft on arrival.
ASRSN:1918245.s: The flight crew detected a foul odor in the cockpit and galley during preflight and takeoff, likely from the APU bleed air. They followed odor isolation procedures by turning off Pack 1 and closing the crossbleed valve, then continued to the destination where Tech Ops met the aircraft.

ASRSN:1918252.n: Low speed rejected T/O (takeoff) at 70 knots due to F/CTL (control) ELAC 2 PITCH FAULT.
ASRSN:1918252.s: The crew rejected takeoff at 70 knots due to an ELAC 2 pitch fault. The aircraft was on the ground during the takeoff roll when the flight control system failure occurred.

ASRSN:1918255.n: Aircraft XZZZZ to ZZZZ1We were on the arrival to Runway XX, Approach Control started to slow us for in trail spacing for the runway. We were being slowed drastically because of spacing so I chose to configure the aircraft early for landing. The aircraft was fully configured gear down Flaps 5 well outside the FAF and roughly around 2,500 feet AGL. After passing the FAF ZZZZZ, and inside roughly 1,700 feet, we got the EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) messages for HYD 1/2 LO PRESS and HYD 1/2 ELEC PUMP FAIL. It was also noted that the PTU (Power Transfer Unit) turned on and the messages cleared themselves momentarily. Seconds later we received HYD 2 LO QTY, I was in control of the aircraft as PF (Pilot Flying) and instructed the First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) to pull up his HYD page on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display), we noticed the quantity was showing ZERO. We were able to quickly diagnose the situation and I called for the QRH, the First Officer did good work beginning to run the procedure, we got through the procedure, and was lead to the loss of HYD System 2 QRH where we briefed the special landing considerations. After being satisfied knowing that we could safely land, it was at this point we concluded our Non Normal procedures. It was my determination and agreeable of the FO (First Officer) that the safest course of action would be to land. At this point we were fully configured for landing and it was decided that was the best scenario to be in, and not to change any configuration. This was the best situation to be in as we were coming up on short final. Runway XX at ZZZZ1 is over 10,000 feet long and we needed roughly 3,900 feet. Even with the landing distance addition for the failure it would be multiplied by 1.66 resulting in needing roughly 7,000 feet, plenty of runway remained and was available.Using my best judgement, we decided the safest course of action due to being fully configured already for landing and on roughly a 4 - 5 mile final was to continue the landing at ZZZZ1 especially with a 10,000 foot runway. We landed NORMALLY, and it was during the roll out, we received the associated flight control failure messages that would be expected with a loss of HYD SYS 2.I was unable to use nose wheel steering, and had reduced braking, however I was able to vacate Runway XX via the high speed taxiway and came to a stop on Taxiway 1, short of runways where we then coordinated with OPS, Ground and Tower to get a tow to the handstand parking.
ASRSN:1918255.s: The flight crew experienced a loss of Hydraulic System 2 pressure and quantity during the final approach to Runway XX. They continued the landing with reduced braking and no nose wheel steering, successfully vacating the runway and taxiing to a stop for a tow.

ASRSN:1918317.n: Material Logistic Specialist on duty in the ZZZ Warehouse Shipping Department was preparing material for the Load Device 3 can to ship to Company Maintenance Base. Material Logistic Specialist came across Airways Bill Parcel which is in a hard sided case. The paperwork on the outside of the box was a hand written note that said send to [shop]. This shop is a Company shop. The box had the address, Name and Vendor Number on the repair order. This is not the appropriate paperwork to ship something. When Material Logistic Specialist opened the case she found a repair order # XXXXXXX that was shipped from ZZZ1 on Airway Bill XXX-XXXXXXXX to ZZZ. There was Hazmat paperwork with the shipment that had been generated. None of the repair order paperwork had a Hazardous Materials sticker attached. When I did some research I discovered that this cleared customs on Date and brought to the base by freight truck on that day [who] took the shipment to ZZZ Warehouse Receiving Dept where it would be sorted to where it would go or be received into inventory.
ASRSN:1918317.s: A Material Logistic Specialist at ZZZ Warehouse discovered a hard-sided case containing a repair order and Hazmat paperwork lacking required Hazardous Materials stickers. The shipment had cleared customs and arrived by freight truck, but the missing stickers indicated improper documentation for shipping hazardous materials.

ASRSN:1918344.n: I was VFR flying up a river. Approaching ZZZ1, I received a vector from ATC (290 heading) directly towards 2 Towers (charted) at an altitude that would have created a conflict had I not climbed. Visual conditions at this time were marginally sufficient to visually pick up the Towers. Fortunately, my systems advised me of the Towers and I initiated a climb to avoid.I find it unsafe that ATC was comfortable, and ambivalent to the fact that they vectored me at a conflicting altitude into terrain. When queried, ATC was unaware that there were Towers in that location. With modern technologies, ATC should be able to be alerted to any conflicts and make an effort to advise - especially when vectoring traffic - to enhance aviation safety.
ASRSN:1918344.s: A VFR pilot received an ATC vector toward two charted towers at a conflicting altitude while approaching ZZZ1. The pilot climbed to avoid the terrain after onboard systems alerted them, noting ATC was unaware of the towers and failed to provide a safe clearance.

ASRSN:1918380.n: Drone lost link, no communication of this. Called ZZZ [TRACON] and they said it lost link. Recommendation- Communicate when a drone looses link. As per the new procedures, a drone is supposed to transition IFR at FL200 from R-XXXX to R-XXXY (back and forth) at level altitude and in communication with ZZZ [Center]. The drone lost comms with ZZZ [TRACON] (controlling agency of R-XXXX) and failed to institute the lost comms procedure. I was informed by my supervisor that if they didn't regain comms at 40 after the hour, he would climb to FL200 and head back to R-XXXY NORDO. At 39 after the hour, I called ZZZ [TRACON] to find out if he had regained comms or if he was executing the lost comms procedure. ZZZ [TRACON] replied 'We lost comms but we are talking to him' and told me he would be climbing up and returning in the next 10 minutes or so. Eventually I got a handoff from ZZZ [TRACON] but couldn't talk to the drone. He was on a different code than in my flight plan, so I changed the code in the flight plan to match his current code, since I couldn't talk to him. Once he exited restricted airspace, he changed his code and the data block was stuck in coast track. ZZZ [TRACON] called me several times to see if I got him. On the east side of our airspace, we can hear him but he can't hear us. He lost comms again about 10 miles inside my airspace, and they also lost data link to the drone. I called ZZZ [TRACON] to see if they had him, and they told me that he had lost the link and was not controllable. The drone turned and descended in my airspace, losing approximately 1,000 ft. and doing a full 360 degree turn. I had traffic for the drone, but I was able to turn the traffic to miss the drone and separation was not lost. I was not able to talk to the drone pilot for several minutes, but he could acknowledge my clearance with an IDENT. He eventually made it back to R-XXXY. If we are planning on running drones routinely though busy military airspace and through departure/arrival corridors to ZZZ [VOR], we should require that they 1) have a working two way radio 2) understand IFR procedures and 3) are able to maintain control of the drone.
ASRSN:1918380.s: An air traffic controller managed a drone that lost communication and control link while transitioning through restricted airspace, causing an uncommanded 360-degree turn and 1,000-foot descent. The controller maintained separation by diverting other traffic, and the drone eventually returned to its destination after regaining limited contact.

ASRSN:1918413.n: Note: I'm submitting this at the request of the Dispatch Chief Pilot, with whom I debriefed after the flight. He asked me to submit a report for data collection purposes. Shortly after an on-time takeoff from ZZZ Runway XXR (about 6,000 feet MSL, while climbing out and bound for ZZZ1, we were advised by Departure Control that a (Company) aircrew from a flight behind us wanted to alert us that we had been venting a very large amount of fuel from our right wing fuel vent, from about the beginning of takeoff roll, and that it had continued for as long as the crew could observe us. My First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) visually confirmed this, stressing that we were indeed venting a lot of fuel. We had heard part of the aircrew's transmission before being advised we were the subject of discussion, and we recalled that the reporting crew sounded calm and professional, but clearly considered it urgent that we understood we were venting fuel at an uncommonly high rate. When flight deck duties permitted, FO (First Officer) used his cell phone to video the venting fuel so I could see it, too. I agreed that it was abnormal, and we coordinated with ATC to level off at 10,000 feet MSL to assess our situation and make a game plan. The high rate of fuel venting appeared unaffected by my power reduction during the level-off at 10,000 feet and would ultimately continue to vent at the same high rate until our center fuel tank was completely empty (over an hour later). There is no checklist for this anomaly, as there was no fuel imbalance (full wing tanks and about 10,000 pounds center tank fuel), and the circumstances did not meet the conditions to qualify as a fuel leak. My FO and I agreed not to proceed to ZZZ1 with an undiagnosed fuel issue while appearing to be jettisoning more fuel that we could afford to lose over the course of an approximately three hour flight. We advised ATC that we still had fuel venting and that we did not need to declare anything, but that we would require holding while formulating a game plan for return to ZZZ. We advised our F/As (First Officer), Dispatch and passengers of the situation and calmly explained to everyone that the venting fuel was the result of a normal aircraft fuel venting function that was simply working overtime for reasons unknown to us.While being vectored and awaiting holding, I noted the current total fuel quantity, kept the power (i.e., engine fuel flow) near constant, hacked the clock and determined how much time it took to burn 1,000 pounds of fuel so we could then subtract what the engines burned in that time frame from the total decrease in fuel quantity, then calculate the approximate rate of venting fuel, which we determined to be about 750 pounds per hour. We accepted holding at the ZZZZZ fix at 8,000 feet, which I considered high enough (above 5,000 feet AGL for fuel dissipation above the ground) and low enough for burning gas quickly, which we did with landing gear down and Flaps 5 after entering holding. We decided to burn fuel down to the new (146,300 pounds) -800 maximum landing weight before considering returning to ZZZ for landing. I was aware that an overweight landing is acceptable if landing data supports it, but I was not willing to consider doing so with the fuel still venting, as we felt we had to assume the fuel would still be venting during landing and taxi (I did not favor the risk of venting warm fuel on very hot concrete after stopping with brakes warmer than necessary from landing overweight). As it happened, the venting stopped immediately when center tank fuel was depleted, which coincided with our total weight being right at the new max landing weight. We then departed holding and landed uneventfully on Runway XX. We never declared anything, but we advised Approach we'd like the Fire Department to look us over after clearing the runway. They did so and observed no problems with our aircraft. I cleared them off, but they then asked if one of them couldfollow us to the gate, which we allowed. Block time was just under two hours. I debriefed by phone with Dispatch/Chief Pilot/Maintenance, put the write up in the logbook, debriefed with local Maintenance and proceeded with my crew to our new gate to fly uneventfully to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:1918413.s: The flight crew experienced excessive fuel venting from the right wing during climb after takeoff from ZZZ, caused by an undiagnosed anomaly that emptied the center tank. They returned to ZZZ, burned fuel to reach maximum landing weight, and landed safely with no damage found by the Fire Department.

ASRSN:1918449.n: During pushback from gate X, ground told air carrier X that 'normally our company stops the push much shorter.' Air carrier X was parked behind us and off our right wing, a shorter push would have allowed them space to get by us. Ground then called and asked if we had communication access to our push crew, to which I answered yes. At this point the push crew had us stopped at the point they intended to end the push. Shortly after ground asked us to push deeper, and I relayed to the Captain who relayed to the push crew. In piecing this together after the fact (since I was on ramp and the captain on intercom with the push crew) we believe right before the request to continue the push deeper from captain to ground crew, the ground crew said 'set brakes.' The Captain did not give 'brakes set pressure normal' verbal to the push crew rather asked them to continue the push deeper. They pushed us a few more feet and then ground called me and said to just stay where we were, which I passed along to the Captain and he passed along to the ground crew. At some point after, the captain said to start both engines - I started the first and before going in to the second start our attention was diverted to air carrier X squeezing through a tight spot off our right wing. The Captain released the crew to disconnect, we received a salute, and the 2nd engine was started. Towards the end of the start, the aircraft started rolling forward, perhaps a few feet at most. We noticed the movement and the Captain immediately brought us to a stop and set the parking brake. The Ground Crew was well clear of the aircraft during movement.
ASRSN:1918449.s: During pushback, conflicting instructions between ground control and the flight crew regarding push distance and brake setting caused the aircraft to roll forward a few feet after engine start. The captain immediately stopped the aircraft and set the parking brake, with no injuries or damage reported as the ground crew was clear.

ASRSN:1918485.n: During the boarding process I was made aware of a mobility scooter to be loaded onto the aircraft. I proceeded to ask what sort of battery was installed in the device and whether it could be removed, which I was advised it was not able to be easily removed and was of a lithium variety. It's been my understanding that we are not able to take any sort of lithium battery in our Cargo Hold and that the battery would have to travel in a cabin. I contacted the On-Call Pilot who advised he would get in touch with Person A to provide further guidance and clarification. Whilst waiting for the return phone-call, I devised a plan to take the wheelchair in its stowed position in the crew bag closet. This seemed to be the best option at the time as it satisfied my understanding that the lithium battery had to travel in the cabin with us.On-Call Pilot and Person A returned my call and advised that we are able to take such a device in the cargo hold provided it met certain criteria. I was not provided any details of the device specifically during the boarding process nor was I notified if it met all the criteria written in our Dangerous Goods Manual. Having found a solution myself, I communicated this to both Person A and On-Call Pilot and continued the flight.Having had the time to read the DG Manual, I'm not entirely sure whether I was actually able to take such device as I did not verify it met: Regulations: DGPM XX-XX.X.X.X, 1.d 'The lithium ion battery must be of a type that successfully passed each test in the Company manual of tests and criteria as specified in 49 CFR XXX.XXX unless approved by the DOT Associate Administrator.'DGPM XX-XX.X.X.X, 1.e'e. Medium and large lithium-metal batteries are forbidden aboard a passenger carrying aircraft.'DGPM XX-XX.X.X.Y'Medium and large lithium-ion or lithium polymer batteries are those which exceed 25 grams of equivalent lithium content or have a capacity rating over 100 watt-hours.The information provided to myself as PIC (Pilot in Command) did not confirm or deny any of the above references, only that the device had previously traveled on Company the day of our departure, and other previous flights.I understand that I may have a misunderstanding or a lack of knowledge in this area and made the decisions based on my commitment to safety. I would like to see further guidance on the carriage of these devices in either our manual and or a crew memo.
ASRSN:1918485.s: The Pilot in Command boarded a mobility scooter with a non-removable lithium battery in the crew closet after initial advice prohibited cargo hold transport. Although later cleared for cargo, the pilot noted uncertainty regarding compliance with specific Dangerous Goods Manual criteria for battery capacity and testing.

ASRSN:1918564.n: Aircraft X, Day 0 was my 4th day. The previous day, I flew a 5 leg day with several delays with a short layover. Upon arriving in ZZZ from ZZZ1, we had to wait in the holding area until the gate became available. The First Officer (FO) and I verified the ramp was clear and we had 3 Marshallers. I followed the Lead Marsaller to the gate. Once he gave me the 'Stop' signal, I set the parking brake and we began the Parking Checklist Procedure. During this procedure, I believed I saw the 'Chocks Inserted' signal, so I released the parking brake. Since the Jet Bridge was moving towards the aircraft, I didn't realize the aircraft began moving. The Marshaller promptly repeated the 'Stop' signal and I quickly pressed the brakes and reset the parking brake. The aircraft rolled forward around 10 feet. There was no injury or any damage to the aircraft. I failed to confirm the 'Chock Insert' signal and after releasing brakes, monitor for aircraft movement for a few seconds.
ASRSN:1918564.s: On Day 4, a pilot released the parking brake at the gate believing chocks were inserted, causing Aircraft X to roll forward 10 feet toward a moving jet bridge. The pilot stopped the aircraft after the marshaller repeated the stop signal; no damage or injuries occurred due to the pilot's failure to confirm the chock signal and monitor movement.

ASRSN:1918612.n: Upon proper run up and leaning for an altitude take off aircraft failed to climb after rotation. Engine was running and no misses, flaps at 2nd position and a climb altitude was established. Using Runway XX, take off appeared normal approximately half way down Runway XX. Upon lift off the aircraft failed to increase in airspeed and to sink. An attempt to turn off runway heading to slightly descending terrain did not help. Upon stall speed this writer made the decision to make an off airport landing. Upon a hard touch down the aircraft rolled out under pilot control to a safe stop. The aircraft did not suffer any prop strike. No other property damage occurred or personal injury. Upon recovery by tow truck to the Hanger at ZZZ it was noted that the wing tanks fuel was leaking, some minor under belly scraps on the tail section and a very slight bump on the rudder had occurred from the hard landing. Also noted were some under belly inspection panels that had been bent slightly from an over active landing gear travel. The final issue was a slight rear passenger door frame bent outward and on its reverse side a small half inch crack. Once the aircraft was parked in the hanger the leaking fuel stopped. The engine was started and warmed up and the mag checks, engine temps and operation were normal. On full run up and leaning the tachometer showed approximately 2400 RPM which is normal for other airports this aircraft has successfully taken off from.
ASRSN:1918612.s: The pilot reported that the aircraft failed to climb after rotation during takeoff from Runway XX, resulting in a controlled off-airport landing. Post-incident inspection revealed fuel leaks, minor structural damage, and a cracked door frame, while engine performance checks remained normal.

ASRSN:1918623.n: We took off from ZZZ. Right after takeoff we got a Low Hydraulic System Warning. The Captain was flying and I ran the checklist to shut the Hyd Pump off and the pressure transfer system off. Captain then gave me the flying responsibilities while he verified the checklist, ran the additional ones for overweight landing and precautionary landing. After nearly 2 hours of flying a holding pattern to burn fuel to be below max landing weight and wait for the weather to clear a bit, we landed uneventfully back at ZZZ and taxied to the gate.
ASRSN:1918623.s: The crew experienced a low hydraulic system warning immediately after takeoff from ZZZ. They executed checklists, held for two hours to burn fuel, and landed uneventfully back at ZZZ.

ASRSN:1918629.n: Prior to approach to ZZZ, cancelled IFR to proceed VFR following [Interstate X] through the canyon and [Interstate Y] northbound. We (the crew) have flown this approach multiple times before, typically directions are follow [Interstate Y] north and turn a left base to final for approach to Runway XY at ZZZ. ZZZ Tower asked, 'Are you familiar with the racetrack pattern?' Both of us, having read numerous articles on 'racetrack patterns' (rounded base to final) recently and having flown very similar approaches to the same runway before, agreed that we were familiar and responded 'affirmative.' I believed we were given a descent to pattern altitude, followed shortly by a clearance to descend from 9000 MSL to 6000 MSL and 'follow the racetrack pattern [Interstate Y] northbound, [local road].' Shortly after initiating descent with gear and 15 degrees of flaps, TCAS alerted to a traffic conflict. We saw a Cessna 172/182 (close enough to read the tail number and remember the paint scheme) pass 12-2 o'clock maybe 500 feet lateral separation very shortly thereafter which prompted me to make a left turn to avoid and increase separation, ATC provided no advisory of this traffic before or after TCAS alert (inside Bravo airspace). Descent continued into rounded left base angling toward final to Runway XY.In hindsight, no traffic sequence (a la 'you're number two, after you complete a left circuit you'll be following a 737') was given, so it was not immediately clear that the 'racetrack pattern' the tower desired was to essentially fly a displaced rectangular course east of the airport (or that traffic separation was required for other traffic landing ahead of us). (This was clarified with ATC on the phone in response to the subsequent warning, they named a road as part of this pattern which they have mentioned before when we've flown a traditional pattern and repeated '[Interstate Y] north, and I think that caused the unknown confusion in the air.) While angling toward a final for Runway XY, right seat pilot noticed one of the two airliners off the right was actually on final to XY, not XXL as initially believed. In response, we turned farther left (east/southeast) as we saw the 737 begin to initiate a go-around. We leveled off around 6000 headed southeast bound and asked the tower for clarification and further instructions. They gave us a left turn to loop around and rejoin [Interstate Y] north, then cleared us for a left base and landing on XY. After explanation via phone call, the tower's initial directions were clarified for future use. While I acknowledge we inadvertently failed to comply with their directions, I believe the following factors contributed to the traffic conflict with the 737: 1) lack of a traffic call-out for the Cessna at the top of descent, resulting in distraction and a preemptive left turn, 2) overly complicated directives from the tower with the use of an ambiguous term ('racetrack pattern'), 3) failure to maintain cleared altitude (6000) due to confusion over landing sequence and perhaps failure to clarify directions we initially thought we understood."
ASRSN:1918629.s: The crew experienced a TCAS alert and near-miss with a Cessna and a 737 while descending to Runway XY at ZZZ. The pilot attributed the conflict to ambiguous "racetrack pattern" instructions, lack of traffic advisories, and confusion over the landing sequence.

ASRSN:1918637.n: Originating flight from ZZZ, one passenger. Flight uneventful. Obtained ATIS at destination facility with tower instructions for left downwind Runway XX. Did feel my pattern altitude 200 feet low. Approach felt stabilized. At time of landing, I had appropriate landing speed. I flared too high and plane dropped/bounced twice. I put full power in for go around and had difficulty maintaining control but was subsequently able to complete return to pattern and safe landing. On review of ForeFlight track log my landing speed likely had decayed too much as well but difficult to ascertain if this was during or after the bounce.After parking at ramp, my wife and I went into town for about 2 hours and returned to depart from ZZZ1 with plan for return leg to home field ZZZ. Run up was good, upon take off from Runway XX, engine sounded good however shortly after take off, power was erratic and I immediately contacted Tower with approval to perform teardrop and return to land on Runway XY. Was able to straighten my return approach, despite pulling power back engine was not responding to input and was maintaining too much power to descend. I had to pull mixture out to descend and was able to land safely although Tower did notify me to extend landing gear.After landing found all prop edges bent which I had failed to notice prior to take off. To prevent/remedy, I would have watched my landing airspeed much more closely and not flared too high or too much. Secondly, after such a landing I would have done better pre-flight and in particular looked at the prop.
ASRSN:1918637.s: The pilot experienced a bounced landing and subsequent go-around due to excessive flare and speed decay, followed by an engine power failure on the next takeoff caused by bent propeller edges. The pilot safely returned to land after using mixture control to descend, noting the propeller damage was undetected during pre-flight.

ASRSN:1918661.n: The pilot lifted off and got to around 50 ft. to do his movement checks before beginning his flight. The UAV began to rotate in a circle, the pilot released his thumbs from the controls and then the UAV did a hard left bank and flew fast and straight for about 700+ ft. at the same height of 50 ft. until it reached a nearby tree line where it crashed into a tree and fell to the ground. There was no damage to property and injury to human. The UAV was quickly located and all of the parts that fell off. Looking at the flight data shows a flyaway with no stick movement of any kind. This is the second time this UAV has had a flyaway.
ASRSN:1918661.s: The pilot experienced a UAV flyaway at 50 ft during post-lift-off checks when the aircraft banked left and crashed into a tree line after 700 ft. Flight data showed no stick input, marking the second such incident for this UAV, with no injuries or property damage reported.

ASRSN:1918662.n: On Day I was hired to take photos of a residential home in Location. The location of the home was about XXX miles away from my home. On my way to the location, the realtor sent me the location of the home. Once I located the house I realized that it was near the airport. Having been so far from home, I made a choice to fly the drone to take photos of the property to have to avoid a return XXX mile trip. I was aware of the location so I stayed at a low altitude and made sure to complete the operation with a few minutes. Due to previous issues in the past requesting permission to fly near that airport, I had trouble requesting access to fly, to which I assumed it would be difficult again. I flew right above the tree line and was finished in about 5 minutes to avoid any possible safety issue with manned aircraft.
ASRSN:1918662.s: A photographer flew a drone near an airport to photograph a residential home, avoiding a long return trip. The operator flew low above the tree line for five minutes without obtaining permission, assuming access would be denied due to past issues.

ASRSN:1918686.n: At FL390 we experience the loss of all B Hydraulic System quantity. Ran appropriate checklists, advised, M/C (Maintenance Crew) and Dispatch. Landed using back-up Electric Flap systems. Asked for a longer final to deal with the slow Alternate Flap system. Landed flaps 15º and red leaders said all looked normal. At 39,000 feet, received Master Caution for low pressure on Engine Driven Hydraulic Pump B. Checked the system quantity and it read zero, performed non normal checklist, advised company, Flight Attendants, and ATC (requested priority handling). Briefed and planned our arrival into ZZZ. Descended and landed without incident. Captain executed the landing.
ASRSN:1918686.s: The crew experienced a total loss of B Hydraulic System quantity at FL390 due to low pressure on the Engine Driven Hydraulic Pump B. They landed safely using the alternate electric flap system with flaps 15º after requesting priority handling and a longer final approach.

ASRSN:1918707.n: As we prepared for taxi, a couple of minutes after the APU was shut down, the FA's (Flight Attendants) called to inform us of strong fumes in the rear of the aircraft. Turned off bleeds and returned to gate. FA's experienced numerous symptoms such as burning eyes, tingling nose and headaches. [They] went to hospital as recommended by their union reps, after examination by paramedics.Second time in three days that I've had a fume event on Aircraft X.Determine the cause of this aircraft's problem and correct it.
ASRSN:1918707.s: Pilots and flight attendants experienced strong fumes in the rear of Aircraft X during taxi preparation after APU shutdown. The crew returned to the gate, and flight attendants were hospitalized with symptoms like burning eyes and headaches, marking the second such event in three days.

ASRSN:1918721.n: Flight from ZZZ to ZZZZ, flying a route down to coast to avoid weather Severe WX. Between ZZZ1 and ZZZZZ Captain did a normal system monitor check. Upon looking at the COND page, he noticed the AFT Cargo Temp at 180 degrees (Steady Green), asked me if I had seen a temp that high, I replied No! We kept an eye on it, over the next 10 minutes, noticed it rising to 188 degrees, then 194 degrees (still Steady Green) where it stayed for the duration of the flight. This made us uncomfortable for normal Cargo Bay temperatures in my 3,000+ hours flying this aircraft at 2 different airlines have never exceeded cabin temperatures during cruise. We simultaneously started looking into what could be a catastrophic problem. I got into the QRH AOM/FOM/and other manuals to look for temperature limitations and fixes. I found none, anywhere. During the same time, Captain got on the Phone with Operations and phone patched to Maintenance Control, where they attempted multiple resets to no success. When Captain got off the phone with Maintenance, he said, 'Well nothing fixed It, and they (Maintenance) said we are on our own.'At that point, we agreed as a crew that we didn't know what was going on down there. We were both not comfortable taking an aircraft with this indication over water, with limited divert options to an international location, and with no company or Contract Maintenance at the destination not knowing what was going on down there. The indication was steady at this point, not rising higher [than] 194 degrees, nor giving any other indications to the back when we notified the Flight Attendants and told them what was going on. At this point, we felt we were not in a land as soon as possible scenario, but in a land as soon as practical scenario but keeping land as soon as possible options available and we decided to divert to ZZZ2. We gave ATC a PAN PAN call since we were going to a divert airport that wasn't our alternate but that we were not at the time an emergency aircraft, we just wanted to have all our bases covered. We notified Dispatch both via phone patch and ACARS. During descent we were cleared the ZZZZZ Arrival to ZZZ2.We were still grossly overweight with a lot of gas, so we referenced the overweight Checklist.
